title: Swap the glemy git dependency for the real Hex release, 0.1.0
context: This repo's gleam.toml depended on glemy via a git dependency pinned to commit f5aa0437 since the split (see glemy's own docs/decisions.jsonl for that decision). glemy published a real 0.1.0 release to Hex shortly after. glemy's own ARCHITECTURE.md always framed the git dependency as a transitional bridge until a real Hex release existed.

options_considered.option: Keep the git dependency, since it already works and there's no forcing function to change it
options_considered.reason: A real Hex release now exists, and this repo's own ARCHITECTURE.md already documented the git dependency as transitional. Delaying the swap only means re-deriving 'why haven't we done this yet' later, for no benefit -- the change is small, low-risk, and immediately verifiable.

decision: Changed gleam.toml's `glemy = { git = "...", ref = "f5aa0437..." }` to `glemy = ">= 0.1.0 and < 0.2.0"`. Re-resolved dependencies (`gleam deps download` correctly reported 'Added glemy v0.1.0 / Removed glemy'), updated the checked-in `manifest.toml` lock, updated ARCHITECTURE.md/CLAUDE.md's own description of the dependency mechanism, and updated the warnings baseline (122 -> 85 warnings).
verification: gleam build/gleam test both targets pass in full (118 Erlang / 125 JavaScript, unchanged), deno task check-warnings passes against the updated baseline, and all three real browser-checks (Tiers/Breakout/Platformer) pass against a live dev server. A fresh GitHub Actions CI run (no local build cache) also passed green, confirming the Hex resolution works from a cold checkout, not just locally.
consequences: Discovered and fixed a real, previously-unnoticed side effect while investigating: the git-dependency commit (f5aa0437) actually predated game removal from glemy's own repo (that removal was a later commit), so this repo had been silently pulling in a stray, unused copy of the game files via the dependency itself the whole time -- harmless (no module-path collisions, since this repo's own game code lives under glemy_games/, not glemy/), but genuinely dead weight, now gone. All 37 warnings that dropped from the baseline traced directly to that stray copy, confirmed individually before updating rather than assumed. Future glemy releases now flow in via ordinary `gleam deps download` within the `>= 0.1.0 and < 0.2.0` range; widening that range (a new minor/major) is its own deliberate decision, not automatic.

title: Add a BEAM-actor multiplayer pilot for Breakout, co-op not competitive
context: glemy/physics and glemy_games/games/breakout already compile and pass gleam test on both the Erlang and JavaScript targets. That makes a server-authoritative multiplayer mode possible without a second, drift-prone physics implementation: the same breakout.tick call that runs client-side in the browser can run server-side on BEAM. No such mode existed yet, and nothing in either repo had ever used gleam_otp/mist/gleam_erlang.

options_considered.option: Real head-to-head Breakout: two paddles on opposite edges, new win condition
options_considered.reason: A genuine game-design change to breakout.Model and its win/lose rules, not a networking change -- out of scope for a pilot meant to prove the room/actor/WebSocket loop itself.

options_considered.option: Co-op: every connected player's held move_left/move_right OR'd into the one existing paddle, breakout.gleam untouched
options_considered.reason: Proves the full server-authoritative loop (OTP room actor, WebSocket protocol, client-side rendering off received snapshots) against already-tested game rules, with zero changes to games/breakout.gleam or its own test suite.

options_considered.option: Always-tick the room on a fixed schedule regardless of whether anyone is connected
options_considered.reason: The first implementation did this. A live two-client smoke test (not gleam test -- an actor/socket loop isn't practically unit-testable) caught the room ticking the ball to Lost and freezing, per breakout.tick's own documented contract, before any player ever got a chance to connect. Switched to pausing simulation while the room's players list is empty and resuming on the next Join.

options_considered.option: Put the new room/session/protocol code in glemy itself as a generic 'net' Shell, symmetric to render.gleam/io.gleam
options_considered.reason: Only one game needs this so far. Matches decision 0058's already-established precedent (glemy/physics/rect.gleam was promoted out of a game only at its second real caller) -- kept entirely inside glemy-games (game_breakout_server.gleam) for now.

decision: Added glemy_games/game_breakout_server.gleam (Erlang-only, mirroring how the existing JS runners are @target(javascript)-gated): a mist HTTP/WebSocket server plus one gleam_otp actor per server holding the single authoritative breakout.Model, ticking games/breakout.tick at a fixed 30Hz and broadcasting JSON snapshots. Added glemy_games/game_breakout_multiplayer.gleam + its _ffi.mjs (JavaScript-only): a thin client that polls input and sends it only on change, and renders whenever a snapshot arrives rather than running its own simulation. Added breakout_multiplayer.html. Added gleam_otp/gleam_erlang/gleam_json/gleam_http/mist to glemy-games' gleam.toml. Both new server-side and client-side wire-protocol functions (merge_inputs, encode_snapshot/encode_welcome, decode_input, server_message_decoder, encode_input) are pub specifically so the pure logic has direct gleam test coverage, separate from the actor/socket wiring around them.
verification: gleam build/gleam test green on both targets (130 Erlang / 129 JavaScript passing, up from 118/125 pre-split-era baseline), deno task check-warnings green against a refreshed baseline. Live end-to-end smoke test against a real running mist server using two independent WebSocket clients: player B, sending no input at all, observed the shared paddle move purely from player A's held input (the actual co-op proof, not inferable from gleam test alone); a brick_destroyed event reached both clients; a third, late-joining connection correctly received in-progress state (remaining bricks, live score, current paddle position) via the welcome payload instead of a fresh game reset. The empty-room free-fall bug above was found by this live test, not by gleam test.
consequences: This is a fixed, single dev-only room (ws://localhost:4001/ws/breakout, no matchmaking, no multiple rooms) -- a real deployment story is a separate future decision. A competitive two-paddle mode remains a distinct, larger piece of work (new Model shape, new win condition) if ever wanted. tools/testdata/expected_warnings.json was refreshed as part of this change; that refresh also absorbed an unrelated, pre-existing staleness (the baseline still had absolute paths from before this repo was relocated from /home/recregt/projects/glemy-games to its current glemy-all/glemy-games location) that had nothing to do with this feature but blocked the same gate. If a second game ever wants multiplayer, the room/session/protocol pieces here are the concrete candidate for promotion into glemy itself as a generic Erlang-target Shell, the same way physics/rect.gleam was promoted at its own second caller (decision 0058).
